findings.text: A 1/4-inch PMMA rod showed steady flame spread at 13.6% O2 in BASS-II, versus 16% O2 blowoff in 1 g: a negative oxygen margin of safety of 2.4% O2.
findings.where: page 18 (Spacecraft Materials Microgravity Research on Flammability, Olson)

findings.text: PMMA rod ignition delay increased significantly near the minimum O2 limit, up to almost 10 times longer than the NASA-STD-6001 standard igniter on-time.
Below a critical opposed-flow velocity, flames over thin fuels could not sustain steady spread; across four thicknesses this velocity did not depend on thickness but rose as O2 decreased.
Most BASS-II flames released well below 100 W, burned fuel rich (global equivalence ratio 1.3 on average), with CO/CO2 ratios an order of magnitude above efficient flue gases.
findings.where: PDF page 19 (report p. 11), section 1.6 Overall Conclusions

findings.text: The three Nomex samples (a fire barrier heavily used on ISS) did not ignite; a wax droplet ejected from a candle typified the flame-spread hazard of melting plastics.

PSI-25.safety_insight: Normal-gravity screening can be non-conservative: the BASS-II team states that 1-g flammability limits for this PMMA material should be de-rated by at least 2.4% O2.
PSI-25.note: Summary Report locations use the PDF page markers, with the printed report page in parentheses. BASS-II Summary Report.pdf.txt is an identical copy. The report also says the model predicted much higher spread rates than observed (section 5.7, PDF p. 71). The fact sheet gives inconsistent BASS-II sample counts (100 samples vs 41 samples/89 test points).

findings.text: Local application of nitrogen suppressant was not adequate for extinguishment: the jet entrains air and sustained the flame even with ambient airflow off, and can even strengthen it.
A 500 cc/min nitrogen flow weakened but did not extinguish a burning PMMA sphere; thick solids store heat, so nitrogen-jet extinction was not possible for the given flow rate.
findings.where: pages 53 and 55 (PMMA sphere wake slide; Summary continued)

findings.text: Cotton-fiberglass fabric, which self-extinguishes in 1-g downward spread, burned steadily in microgravity opposed flow, spreading fastest at flows around 10 to 15 cm/s.
At about 10 cm/s, flame spread was 2.55 mm/s concurrent versus 1.21 mm/s opposed; concurrent spread rose linearly with flow, with quenching extinction around 1 cm/s.
Flames were especially sensitive to airflow of 0 to 5 cm/s; even the smallest flames on acrylic slabs burned over 5 minutes before self-extinguishing.

PSI-26.safety_insight: A tiny flame might burn undetected for a long time and flare up if airflow suddenly increases, while a local nitrogen jet can entrain air and sustain it.
PSI-26.note: The mini-book credits the suppression findings to the BASS experiment in general, without separating BASS and BASS-II. Also reported: Ultem and Nomex HT90-40 did not burn at 21-22% O2 and about 15 cm/s, but Nomex-III did (Overview, page 30). 41 samples and 115 burns were completed (Overview, page 10).

findings.text: FLEX-2 burned droplets at 0.5 to 3.0 atm and 0.1 to 0.4 O2 mole fraction, with about 2 minutes of settling and 1 to 5 s of igniter power.
FLEX-2 images compare sooting propensity in different diluents for ethanol burning in 30% oxygen at 2.4 atm.
The SRD specifies sooting n-decane and nominally non-sooting ethanol as pure fuels, plus four binary mixtures, two chosen to develop surrogate models for JP8 aviation fuel.
findings.where: PDF page 39 (SRD p. 33), section 5.1.1 Test Fuels

findings.text: FLEX-2 tests fall into four groups (pure fuel, fuel mixture, convective flow, binary droplet array), each with 30 to 60 separate tests.
PSI holds 40 FLEX-2 Experiment Data records organized by test matrix (e.g., binary array, quiescent, surrogate fuel), with raw data and images per test point.

PSI-68.safety_insight: Indirect: FLEX-2 targets fundamental liquid-fuel combustion rather than fire safety, but its flame-extinction and soot data help validate droplet combustion models.
PSI-68.note: No FLEX-2 flight results are stated in the local documents. The SRD is a pre-flight requirements document, and fichas_7.txt lists only publication titles. The SRD O2 range (0.17-0.30) differs from the catalog approach (0.1-0.4). Mini-book page 36 credits the LOI and cool-flame findings to FLEX and FLEX-2 together; they are listed under PSI-69.

findings.text: FLEX identified radiative and diffusive extinction limits for heptane and methanol droplets, and a limiting oxygen index significantly lower than in normal gravity and lower than previously predicted.
After radiative extinction of the visible hot flame, large alkane droplets kept vaporizing at the same rate, sustained by a lower-temperature cool flame that can burn for a prolonged time.
This second-stage low-temperature burning had never been observed in over 50 years of microgravity droplet combustion experiments; more recent tests showed similar behavior in n-octane and n-decane.
findings.source: PSI-69_Presentations_Cool Flames in Space, a Hot Prospect on Earth!.pdf.txt

findings.text: An analysis of FLEX n-heptane data estimated second-stage burn temperatures of 1000-1400 K, assuming a 50% heat release rate.
Cool flames produce partially oxidized fuel and combustible vapor that can re-ignite to hot flames, seen with decane; widely used kinetic models do not accurately predict cool-flame extinction.
findings.source: PSI-69_Presentations_Cool Flames in Space, a Hot Prospect on Earth!.pdf.txt

PSI-69.safety_insight: In space, terrestrial inert-gas suppressant standards lack the same safety margin, and after a hot droplet flame goes out, a cool flame can persist and generate vapor that can re-ignite.
PSI-69.note: The safety insight combines mini-book page 12 (suppressant safety margin) and Cool Flames presentation page 22. Mini-book page 36 groups FLEX with FLEX-2; heptane and methanol are the FLEX fuels (page 12). No numeric LOI value appears in the documents reviewed. Finding 4 is an analysis by Nayagam et al. as reported by Farouk and Dryer.

findings.text: Saffire-I burned a 0.4 m by 1 m cotton-fiberglass sample, ignited by hot wire; previously, the largest fire experiment conducted in space was about index-card size.
The sample, about 0.94 m by 0.4 m, is at least an order of magnitude larger in both dimensions than any prior low-g flame spread experiment, with 20 cm/s airflow.
findings.source: PSI-98_Science Documents_SAFFIRE Objectives, Development and Status.pdf.txt

findings.text: Specific aim: determine how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low gravity and whether it reaches a steady-state spread rate.
Measured with two cameras, thermocouples for flow, flame and plume temperatures, two radiometers for flame radiation, solid-state pressure, CO2 and O2 sensors, and two anemometers.
Saffire-I started about 1 day after Cygnus undocked and ran automatically; downlink time limited data to a maximum of 20 gigabits.

PSI-98.safety_insight: Burning a 0.4 m by 0.94 m fabric sample in an uncrewed Cygnus lets NASA study realistic spacecraft fire growth without crew risk, informing fire-emergency protocols.
PSI-98.note: Saffire-I results (growth or spread rates) are not in the local documents. The Objectives paper was written before the burn, and the MergeResult spreadsheet only lists image files. The fact sheet says the mission was completed in July 2016. Sample length is 1 m in the fact sheet and about 0.94 m elsewhere.

findings.text: Saffire-II carried nine 5 cm x 29 cm samples, the size used in NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, to quantify how low-g flammability limits differ from normal gravity.
findings.source: PSI-99_Science Documents_SAFFIRE Objectives, Development and Status.pdf.txt

findings.text: Samples were four silicone (0.25 to 1.02 mm), two SIBAL fabric (0.33 mm, at 20 and 30 cm/s), PMMA-to-Nomex, and structured and flat PMMA, both 10 mm thick.
findings.source: PSI-99_Science Documents_SAFFIRE Objectives, Development and Status.pdf.txt

findings.text: Materials were chosen because their normal-gravity Maximum Oxygen Concentration limits indicate burning just above and below 21% O2; some were expected to burn, others may not.
findings.source: PSI-99_Science Documents_SAFFIRE Objectives, Development and Status.pdf.txt

findings.text: Launched in October 2016 aboard Cygnus and completed Nov. 27, 2016; samples included cotton-fiberglass, Nomex and the acrylic glass used for spacecraft windows.
PSI holds image records for all nine samples (S1-S9) plus pre-flow and post-flow sets, from two cameras.

PSI-99.safety_insight: Burning materials rated near 21% O2 in 1-g tests checks whether normal-gravity NASA screening (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) correctly predicts which spacecraft materials burn in low gravity.
PSI-99.note: No Saffire-II results (which samples burned, spread rates) are in the local documents. Sample length is 29 cm in the Readme and Objectives paper but 25 cm in the SAFFIRE-I Operations document. The Objectives paper's tentative dates (as of 4/30/2016) differ from the fact sheet.

findings.text: Saffire-III used the same SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric as Saffire-I, but at a flow velocity of 30 cm/s instead of 20 cm/s; flow was concurrent or opposed.
Saffire-III burns a single large sample, about 0.4 m wide by 0.94 m tall, recording and compressing the entire burn; at most 20 gigabits can be downlinked.
Specific aim: determine how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low gravity and whether it reaches a steady-state spread rate.
Launched April 18, 2017 on the seventh Orbital ATK resupply mission; ignition was planned after Cygnus departed the station in early June, before destructive reentry.
The run starts about half a day after Cygnus undocks, with the vehicle in free-drift mode; Saffire stays unpowered during launch, berthing and unberthing.

PSI-100.safety_insight: Burning the Saffire-I fabric again at 30 instead of 20 cm/s targets how airflow changes large-fire growth in low gravity, to inform spacecraft fire-emergency protocols.
PSI-100.note: No Saffire-III results are in the local documents; the MergeResult spreadsheets only list image and raw data files. The Objectives paper's tentative dates (launch 30-Dec-2016, operations 3-Mar-2017) differ from the fact sheet (launch April 18, 2017).
